title: Instemmen
excerpt: Instemmen (voting in) is the moment a Dutch student house or dispuut decides which new first-years can join.
example: After a tense evening they decided to vote her into the dispuut.
text: After getting to know the candidates, the members of a student house, dispuut or association vote on who gets in. It can be exciting, emotional and very late. Once you are voted in, there is usually a party.

title: Internacho
excerpt: Internacho is the nickname Dutch students give to international students. Yes, that probably means you.
example: As an internacho she found it hard at first to keep up with all the abbreviations.
text: The word is used for international students in a mostly Dutch student world. It is usually meant in a friendly, teasing way. And now that you are reading this dictionary, you will soon know more Dutch slang than most Dutch students.

title: Internet personality
excerpt: An internet personality is someone who got famous mainly through being online.
example: "He's not an actor or a singer. He's just an internet personality with two million followers."
text: Think of creators, streamers, meme characters and people who got famous from one viral moment. They didn't get known through TV or film, but through the internet. Lots of them make good money with it.

title: Internship
excerpt: An internship is temporary work to get to know a job or company from the inside.
example: "This semester I have an internship at an agency in Amsterdam. Finally some money."
text: An internship can be paid or unpaid. Students do one to get real experience and fill up their CV. Sometimes you roll straight into a job afterwards. In Dutch it is called a stage, and many programmes require one.

title: Introductieweek
excerpt: The introductieweek is the welcome week where new students get to know their city, studies and student associations.
example: During the introductieweek she met her future housemates right away.
text: You do activities and find out what really suits you. It isn't mandatory, but it is one of the easiest ways to make friends fast. Every city has its own name for it, like EL CID in Leiden. It is the Dutch version of Freshers' Week.

title: IRL
excerpt: IRL stands for in real life. Not online.
example: "We've been texting for weeks, but we've never met IRL."
text: With IRL you separate online life from real life. Online friends, events or identities can be very different IRL. Someone who is online way too much gets told to touch grass.

title: Italiaans afscheid
excerpt: An Italiaans afscheid (Italian goodbye) is a goodbye where you come back at least three times to say bye once more.
example: She was already at the door, but came back three more times for her Italiaans afscheid.
text: You keep walking back to your friends for one last goodbye before you actually leave. Hugs, one more story, another hug. The opposite is the houdini, where you vanish without saying anything.

title: It's giving
excerpt: It's giving is used to describe the vibe or impression something gives off.
example: "That coat with the fur collar? It's giving rich aunt on a ski trip."
text: After it's giving there is usually a comparison. Sometimes people leave the sentence open: "it's giving". Then they mean something looks great. It is used a lot for fashion and memes. It comes from ballroom and drag culture.

title: IYKYK
excerpt: IYKYK stands for if you know, you know. A joke or reference only insiders get.
example: She posted a photo of a traffic cone on the roof of the student house, with the caption: "IYKYK."
text: With IYKYK you show there is a story behind something that not everyone knows. Inside jokes, shared experiences or niche references. Whoever gets it laughs. The rest stays curious.

title: Jaarclub
excerpt: A jaarclub (year club) is a group within a Dutch student association made up of members from the same year.
example: Every month her jaarclub went out for dinner in town.
text: A jaarclub is common at associations with a horizontal setup, where you mostly hang out with people from your own year. You join in your first year and often stay friends for life. Short version: JC.

title: Jägerbomb
excerpt: A Jägerbomb is a popular party drink: a shot of Jägermeister dropped into a glass of energy drink.
example: At the bar they ordered five Jägerbombs for the group in one go.
text: The shot glass of Jägermeister gets dropped into the energy drink, and then you down the lot. Fast, sweet and loud. A favourite on nights out. Just maybe not the night before an exam.

title: Jasje dasje
excerpt: Jasje dasje (jacket tie) is a semi-formal Dutch student dress code: a blazer, a tie and jeans.
example: For the borrel everyone had to show up in jasje dasje.
text: It is worn at special events within a student association. A bit more relaxed than a full suit, but you still look the part. If an invite says jasje dasje, leave the hoodie at home.

title: JC
excerpt: JC is short for jaarclub, a group of friends from the same year within a Dutch student association.
example: "Are you coming with the JC this weekend?" she asked in the group chat.
text: The short version is mostly used in texts and between members. Nobody has time to type jaarclub every time. Your JC is often your second family during your student years.

title: JOMO
excerpt: JOMO stands for joy of missing out. The pleasure of staying in on purpose and skipping something.
example: "Everyone's going out, but I'm on the couch with tea and a series. Pure JOMO."
text: JOMO is the playful opposite of FOMO. You feel no pressure to be everywhere. You actually enjoy time for yourself. Especially after a busy week, JOMO can be wonderful.

title: Junior
excerpt: In the US, a junior is a student in the third year of high school or university.
example: "When I was a junior during my exchange, I was finally allowed to live off campus."
text: In the US every study year has its own name: freshman, sophomore, junior and senior. Junior is the third year. The word has other meanings too, like a junior employee. But in student land it means year three.

title: Kaasschaaf
excerpt: Kaasschaaf (cheese slicer) is a not very flattering Dutch student word for someone who is clumsy in bed.
example: "So was he really such a kaasschaaf?" she asked her friend, giggling.
text: Picture a cheese slicer and you can guess the details. The nickname usually goes to an inexperienced first-year. And it spreads through the friend group faster than you would like.

title: Kantelen
excerpt: Kantelen (to tip over) has two meanings: a night that turns out amazing, or downing a drink in one go.
example: "Just kantelen that beer already," his friend said impatiently.
text: A night that kantelt is a big success, just like escaleren. Kantelen a beer means tipping it back in one go, the same as adten. So kantelen a few beers usually makes the night kantelen too.

title: Kapstokhertje
excerpt: A kapstokhertje (coat rack deer) hangs around the coats at the end of a party, hoping to leave with someone.
example: At the exit a kapstokhertje was still looking around to see who else was going home.
text: At the end of a party or borrel this person lingers by the coat rack. Just in case someone wants company on the way home. It is a play on hertje, the corps word for an attractive woman.

title: Kings Cup
excerpt: Kings Cup is a card drinking game. Every card comes with its own rule or task.
example: "Whoever draws the fourth king has to drink the whole Kings Cup."
text: The rules are different in every friend group. That is part of the fun. The game is also called Ring of Fire. In the Netherlands lots of students play their own version, called Kingsen.

title: KMT
excerpt: KMT ("kennismakingstijd") is the official introduction period where a feut gets to know a Dutch student association.
example: During the KMT she had to do tasks with her fellow feuten every night.
text: KMT is the official name for what people used to call ontgroening. During this period a feut becomes a sjaars and gets to know the association. Don't confuse it with the introductieweek, which is organised by universities for everyone.

title: Knor
excerpt: Knor (oink) is what members of a Dutch corps call students who are not members of the corps.
example: "Easy there, knor," a corps member called out to a passing student.
text: Corps members use it for anyone outside their association. Some say it stands for "kent niet onze regels": doesn't know our rules. It is a bit snobby. Most people who get called knor wear it with pride.

title: Kompaan
excerpt: Kompaan is a Dutch word for a mate or buddy.
example: "Hey kompaan, come sit with us," he called from the couch.
text: It is mostly used among friends as a casual, friendly way to address someone. A bit old-fashioned, a bit funny. Like calling someone "comrade" with a wink.

title: Kot
excerpt: Kot is the Belgian word for a student room.
example: In Leuven she invited her friends over to her kot for a movie night.
text: Kot is mostly used in Flanders. Students live "op kot" during the week and go home to their parents at the weekend. Dutch students would say studentenkamer, or just thuis. In English you would say student room or dorm.

title: Krokant
excerpt: Krokant (crispy) describes an awkward vibe, or the awkward feeling you are left with afterwards.
example: After that comment the atmosphere at the table suddenly got very krokant.
text: The word describes an uncomfortable or tense situation, like a borrel that just isn't working. You can also feel krokant yourself after embarrassing yourself. Close to cringe.

title: Kruipafstand
excerpt: Kruipafstand (crawling distance) is Dutch student slang for something that is really, really close by.
example: The room ad proudly said: supermarket within kruipafstand.
text: It is even closer than a stone's throw. Close enough to crawl to after a big night out. Students use it in room ads, for example when the house is near the university library or the super.

title: Kwarrel
excerpt: A kwarrel (quality scharrel) is a casual fling where there is also an emotional click.
example: With her kwarrel she could finally have a real conversation instead of just hooking up.
text: A kwarrel goes a step further than a scharrel. Besides the physical side, you also talk about feelings and you can count on each other. Not a relationship, but not nothing either. Very situationship.

title: L
excerpt: L stands for loss. You use it for something that goes wrong or someone who embarrasses themselves.
example: "I slept through my exam. Massive L."
text: Taking an L means you lose or something ends badly. Telling someone to "take the L" means they should just accept the loss. The opposite is a W.

title: Labo
excerpt: Labo has two meanings among Dutch students: a lame drinker who won't keep up, or the long receipt from the supermarket.
example: "What a labo," they joked when he left his beer untouched for the third time.
text: At a borrel, a labo ("laffe borrelaar") refuses to adten or drinks way too slowly. At the supermarket, labo stands for "lange bon", the extra long receipt from the self-checkout. Two very different things, one word.

title: Lapswans
excerpt: Lapswans is a casual, cheerful Dutch way to say goodbye.
example: "Lapswans everyone, I'm off," he called when leaving the borrel.
text: You use it when leaving, like "see ya" or "laters". It is used more widely than just among students. The opposite of a houdini, where you leave without saying anything at all.

title: Last call
excerpt: Last call is the final round. The moment the bar announces you can order one more time.
example: "Last call!" the bartender shouted. The whole group ran to the bar.
text: When last call happens depends on the bar and its licence. After that you have a little time to finish your drink. In the Netherlands the lights often go on as a sign it is time to go. Dutch students then go afpilsen at home.

title: Lecture
excerpt: A lecture is a class where a lecturer or professor explains things to a big group of students.
example: "The lecture starts at half past eight. I'll watch the recording later."
text: In a lecture you mostly listen. There is less room for discussion than in a seminar or tutorial. Sometimes there are questions or polls. In Dutch it is called a hoorcollege.

title: Leenstelsel
excerpt: The leenstelsel (loan system) was the Dutch system where students paid for their studies with a loan from DUO.
example: Because of the leenstelsel she finished her studies with a big debt to DUO.
text: Between 2015 and 2023 Dutch students got no free basic grant. Instead they borrowed money they had to pay back later. The students from those years call themselves the pechgeneratie, the unlucky generation. Since 2023 there is a basic grant again.

title: Left on delivered
excerpt: Left on delivered means your message arrived, but hasn't been opened or answered yet.
example: "I texted him yesterday. Still left on delivered."
text: With left on delivered you don't know if the other person saw your message. That makes it nerve-racking. It mostly matters in dating, where reply time is sometimes seen as a sign of interest. Even worse is left on read.

title: Left on read
excerpt: Left on read means someone read your message but didn't reply.
example: "Blue ticks, but no reply. She left me on read."
text: Lots of apps show when a message has been read. That makes no reply feel extra awkward. Sometimes someone just has no time. Sometimes it is the first sign of ghosting.

title: Let him cook
excerpt: Let him cook means: let him do his thing. Something good might come out of it.
example: "He wants to have a barbecue on the third floor balcony." "Let him cook."
text: You say it when someone explains a plan, makes a joke or tries something weird. Give it a chance. It can be sincere, but also ironic. Of course it works for "let her cook" too.

title: Level up
excerpt: Level up means improving yourself, in skills, lifestyle or situation.
example: "First a mattress on the floor, now a real bed. My room just levelled up."
text: The term comes from games, where your character goes up a level. Now you see it a lot in self-improvement and motivation content. A big level up in your looks is called a glow-up.

title: Life hack
excerpt: A life hack is a smart little trick that makes an everyday task easier.
example: "Life hack: wrap a wet tea towel around your beer and put it in the freezer for ten minutes."
text: The internet is full of life hacks. Some are really useful. Others are complicated solutions to problems nobody had. Students are champions of creative life hacks on a tiny budget.

title: Lightweight
excerpt: A lightweight is someone who gets drunk after just a few drinks.
example: "Two beers and he's already dancing on the table. What a lightweight."
text: How much you can handle depends on your body, food, habits and more. Lightweight is usually said as a tease. The opposite is a heavyweight. There is nothing wrong with needing just a little.

title: Lit
excerpt: Lit means something is really cool, busy or full of energy. Mostly about parties.
example: "The party last night was so lit. Even the police stopped by."
text: Lit describes a night or place full of energy. It can also mean someone is drunk or high. But on social media people usually just mean something was really good or lively. It is close to fire.

title: Living my best life
excerpt: Living my best life means you are fully enjoying life and doing what makes you happy.
example: She posted a photo with a cocktail by the pool: "Living my best life."
text: The phrase often goes under holiday photos or in captions. Usually sincere, but sometimes ironic. For example under a photo of instant noodles on a Tuesday night.

title: LMAO
excerpt: LMAO stands for laughing my ass off. Something is extremely funny.
example: "He fell off his chair during the praeses' speech. LMAO."
text: LMAO is stronger and ruder than LOL. You use it for things that make you laugh really hard. There is also ROFL: rolling on the floor laughing. Then you are literally on the ground.

title: LMK
excerpt: LMK stands for let me know.
example: "We're having dinner at eight. LMK if you're coming."
text: With LMK you ask someone to get back to you later. A decision, an update or some info. It is short, easy and used a lot in group chats. Dutch students would just send a dapri.

title: Loca
excerpt: Loca is Dutch slang for location. Short for "locatie".
example: "Has anyone picked a loca for the borrel yet?" she asked impatiently in the group chat.
text: You mostly see it in group chats where the plan still needs a place. Once the loca is set, people react with a bee emoji to say they are coming. That is called bij.

title: Locked in
excerpt: Being locked in means you are completely focused on one thing. No distractions, just going.
example: "Phone in the drawer, coffee ready. Today I'm locked in for my exam."
text: The term comes from sports and gaming, where players are locked in when they are fully in the game. Now you use it for studying, working out or work. You can also say it as a call to action: time to lock in.

title: LOL
excerpt: LOL stands for laughing out loud.
example: "I thought the exam was next week. LOL."
text: LOL started as an abbreviation for laughing. Now people also use it to make a message feel lighter. Even when they are not laughing at all. Fun fact: in Dutch "lol hebben" just means having fun.

title: Lore
excerpt: Lore is the background story behind someone or something. Usually full of drama and details.
example: "Wait, why don't they talk anymore? I need to know the lore."
text: Lore comes from games and fantasy stories, where it describes the history of a world. Now people use it for friendships, exes and house drama. Someone with a lot of lore has been through a lot.

title: Louter
excerpt: Louter is a Dutch word for nothing but, purely or only.
example: "I'm doing it louter for fun," she said when someone asked about her motivation.
text: It is often used to put extra weight on something, without anything special behind it. Slightly formal, which makes it funny in casual conversations. Students love using fancy words for silly things.

title: Love bombing
excerpt: Love bombing is overwhelming someone with attention, love and compliments at the start, sometimes to gain control.
example: "After one week of dating he already said 'I love you' and showed up with flowers every day." That feels like love bombing.
text: Not every enthusiastic start is love bombing. It is about it feeling over the top and manipulative. Often distance or control follows later. So a very fast, intense start can be a red flag.

title: Lowkey
excerpt: Lowkey means a little, secretly or without making a big deal of it. The opposite of highkey.
example: "I actually think his new song is lowkey pretty good."
text: With lowkey you tone something down or admit something you would rather not say out loud. A lowkey party is small and quiet. Being lowkey in love means you are not telling everyone yet.
